<meta>continues from previous page: to go a thousand paces: go with him another two.</meta> <margin>Enemies must be loved.</margin> Love your enemies, and do good to those who hate you: and pray for those who persecute and slander you: so that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise over the good and the bad and rains upon the just and the unjust. You reply: He did not say those things to me. He said them to the apostles: he said them to the perfect. Did you not hear: "so that you may be children of your Father"? If you do not desire to be a child of God, the <term>lex</term> <gloss>divine law</gloss> does not apply to you. Although a person is not even good who does not wish to be perfect. Receive this also: if you do not desire a reward, the commandment is nothing to you. For it follows: <margin>Luke 6</margin> For if you love those who love you, what reward will you have? It is as if he were to say: none. For doing that is not a virtue, but not doing it is a crime. Nothing is owed to either side when like is returned for like. <margin>Paul, the legal expert.</margin> Listen to Paul, the great expert and interpreter of Christian laws. <margin>Romans 12</margin> Bless those who persecute you: bless, and do not curse. Returning evil to no one for evil. If it is possible, as far as it depends on you, live in peace with all people. Do not defend yourselves, dearly beloved, but give place to wrath. <margin>Deuteronomy 32</margin> For it is written: Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord. But if your enemy is hungry, feed him. If he is thirsty, give him a drink. For in doing this, you will heap coals of fire upon his head <note>This biblical metaphor refers to making an enemy feel the burning heat of shame, which may lead them to repentance.</note>. Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good. 

What then will happen, you ask, if I nourish the insolence of another with my gentleness, and by bearing an old injury, I invite a new one? <margin>It is more fitting for a Christian to suffer injuries than to cause them.</margin> If you can either escape or drive away the evil without doing evil yourself, no one forbids you from doing so. Otherwise, beware of saying: it is easier to do <note>meaning to commit an injury</note> than to suffer it. If you can, correct the situation, either by overwhelming the person with kindness or conquering them with mildness. If it must be otherwise, it is better for one to perish than both. It is better for you to grow rich by the gain of patience than for both to become evil through mutual retaliation. <margin>The decree of Christianity.</margin> Therefore, let it be a Christian decree: to compete with all in love, mildness, and kindness. In matters of contention, detraction, insult, and injury, one should yield willingly even to the lowest of people. But you say that he is unworthy of having good done to him or being yielded to. Yet it is worthy of you to do it, and worthy is Christ, for whose grace it is done. They say: I do not wish to harm anyone, nor will I suffer myself to be harmed. On the contrary, you who have been harmed, forgive the offense from your heart, taking care that there is nothing for which anyone... <note>The text breaks off here and continues on the next page.</note>

<summary>Erasmus argues that the command to love and forgive enemies applies to all Christians, not just the apostles. He uses the writings of Paul to show that responding to evil with kindness is a spiritual victory that leads to the growth of the soul.</summary>
<keywords>Sermon on the Mount, forgiveness, Paul the Apostle, retaliation, patience, Christian ethics, charity, non-resistance</keywords>
